storm.summary_layperson: A cluster of showers and thunderstorms about 37 miles southwest is tracking toward the cove and should arrive around 5 PM; unlike many summer storms here, the Sound's cooling effect has already faded for the day, so expect an impact similar to inland towns rather than a locally weakened storm.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The marine layer that often blunts storms here is weak today (6.8°F air-water gap) and is projected to drop below the protective threshold by about 4:41 PM — before this cell arrives — so no local buffer is expected this evening.
storm.detail_html:
Radar (KOKX) shows a cluster of showers/storms near 41 dBZ about 37 miles southwest of the cove, tracking north-northeast at roughly 28 kt. That puts arrival at the cove around 5:05 PM, with a window of 4:47–5:22 PM (high confidence — this is a well-tracked, fast-moving system).

The Sound's marine layer, which can often choke down approaching storms, is weak and fading fast today. The air-water gap is only 6.8°F right now (water 76°F vs air 82°F), and the hour-by-hour trend model shows it dropping below the 5°F protective threshold by about 4:41 PM — before this cell even arrives. So the usual Sound-blunts-it discount does not apply to this storm.

The sea breeze isn't a factor either: current coastal wind is a weak, immature southwesterly flow (only 44% of coastal stations reporting southerly), and because the storm itself is also approaching from the southwest, it isn't opposing the storm's track the way an onshore sea breeze normally would. No discount from that mechanism either.

Net effect: the cove should expect an outcome similar to surrounding towns — moderate risk, not a locally muted one. CAPE is modest (1040 J/kg), which favors weakening on its own atmospheric merits, but that's a general factor, not a cove-specific advantage today.

What would change the call: if this cell weakens on radar before closing inside 25 miles, or if a stronger, warned cell develops behind it. Watch the KOKX loop through 5 PM.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell about 37 mi SW closing at 27 kt; it's arriving after the marine layer has already faded, so expect it near full strength with no Sound-driven weakening.

wind.tactics_blurb: Sea breeze reinforced by the background southerly — expect SW-SSW 5–7 kt building through early evening, then going light and soft after the thermal collapses near sunset. Pressure is fairly even across the cove with a slight edge toward the mouth/east shore; start mid-line and work the building right shift early, then expect a soft, wandering finish.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Today classifies as an A+ regime — sea breeze reinforced by the background gradient wind. The air-water temperature gap (deltaT) is 6.8°F, above the 5°F threshold needed for a thermal sea breeze to build, and the background gradient is a light onshore southerly (7.2 kt mean, from the well-sited airport network) rather than calm or offshore — so instead of fighting the thermal, the gradient reinforces it.

Current RYC obs (Riverside YC, ground truth for the cove): SSW 209° at 2.9 kt, 10-min avg 3.3 kt, gusting 4.6 kt — still light and building. That's consistent with an A+ day that hasn't fully filled yet this early. Widen the lens to the western-LIS coastal cluster and the picture agrees: median direction SW 222°, 44% of coastal stations already reporting southerly.

⚠️ HRRR/obs divergence: the model's f01 surface wind forecasts SE 129°, but stations right now read SW 222° — a 93° gap. The deltaT-scaled veer correction that normally reconciles this needs an 8°F gap to trigger, and today's is only 6.8°F, so the correction wasn't applied. Trust the observed SW/SSW axis over the raw HRRR numbers for this window; HRRR's own hourly sequence (SE→E→E→S, all under 5 kt) also looks like a model that hasn't resolved this sea breeze well.

Direction sits on the classic S–SSW sea-breeze axis for this stretch of coast, which runs straight up the cove's own N–S opening — expect fairly even pressure across the course, with a slight edge toward the mouth and east shore (less shelter there on SW-ish flow). It's early enough in the cycle that the first couple hours will feel like a persistent right-building shift rather than a tactical oscillation; once the thermal matures, if it's still running, oscillations become more playable.

Because this is a reinforced (A+) day, the wind should hold roughly 30–60 minutes past the normal sea-breeze collapse — sunset is 7:48 PM, so don't expect it to just vanish at sundown. But the thermal component is going, and the gradient remnant behind it is light (mean 7.2 kt at the airports, lighter still at RYC), so by the 9–10 PM end of this window expect a soft, possibly wandering breeze in the 3–5 kt range — plan for the race to go from a building sweet-spot breeze early to a light/drifter finish.

Data note: HRRR only returned usable hourly output through 7 PM (f05–f12 fetch failures); the 8–10 PM rows above are extrapolated from the A+ regime framework (gradient-reinforced hold, gradual thermal collapse) rather than raw model data.
